before.exam_tip_html: On a 12-mark Discuss question about stratification, the most common error is giving only a functionalist account of Davis and Moore without any counter-perspectives. The mark scheme rewards candidates who present arguments for the statement (citing Davis and Moore’s meritocratic argument) and arguments against (citing Marxist exploitation theory or feminist critiques of patriarchal reward structures). A Mastering-tier answer will name at least two contrasting perspectives with sociological vocabulary (meritocracy, bourgeoisie, patriarchy, ascribed status) and close with a supported judgement about which perspective offers the most convincing explanation — not simply listing both sides.

On a 12-mark Discuss question about family functions, the most common mistake is giving a one-sided answer — listing what functionalists say and stopping there. The mark scheme rewards candidates who present the functionalist view (Murdock’s four functions, Parsons’s two irreducible functions) AND the challenges to it from at least one other perspective (feminist critique of the expressive/instrumental role division, or Zaretsky’s Marxist critique). Name your theorists: “Parsons argued that…” and “Oakley, however, contended that…”. Always end with a supported judgement: explain which perspective you find most convincing and why, using evidence. On a 2-mark Define question, give a definition in sociological language — for “primary socialisation”, write “the earliest stage of socialisation occurring within the family, through which children learn the basic norms and values of their culture”, not just “learning things as a child”.

For a 4-mark Describe question on factors affecting life chances, avoid listing all seven factors without developing any. The mark scheme rewards depth, not breadth. Choose two or three factors and describe how each affects life chances using sociological vocabulary: material deprivation, glass ceiling, ageism, institutional racism, patriarchy. On a 12-mark Discuss, make sure you compare perspectives — if the question is about class and life chances, a Mastering answer will contrast the functionalist view (meritocratic rewards) with the Marxist view (structural reproduction of inequality) and name Devine’s study as evidence about working-class aspirations and class identity.

On a 12-mark Discuss about whether schools reproduce inequality, the strongest answers present Bowles and Gintis’s correspondence principle clearly (name the study, name the year, explain the mechanism), then evaluate it from at least one contrasting perspective. The most common error is to describe the correspondence principle without explaining why it reproduces inequality — the key is the hidden curriculum: the implicit socialisation into accepting hierarchy and obedience. Examiners want to see you explain the mechanism, not just name it.

For 3-mark Identify and Describe questions, remember the structure: one sentence to identify the concept (e.g. ‘the hidden curriculum’), then two sentences to develop and explain. Candidates who only give a one-line identification score 1 out of 3.

For a 4-mark Describe question on Walby’s six structures of patriarchy, do not simply list all six without explanation — this scores in the lower band. The mark scheme rewards depth: name two or three structures, describe each one clearly and link them to examples (the glass ceiling and gender pay gap for paid work; the double shift for household production; male violence and Heidensohn’s work on female conformity for the violence structure). On a 12-mark Discuss about patriarchy or gender inequality, always contrast Walby’s feminist analysis with the functionalist view (gender roles as functional specialisation) and/or the Marxist view (inequality rooted in class conflict). Close with a judgement about whether patriarchy or class conflict better explains gender inequality in contemporary Britain.

The most common error on methods questions is evaluating a method generically rather than in context. If a question asks you to evaluate the use of official statistics to study crime, the mark scheme rewards points specific to crime research: the dark figure, the problem of unreported crimes, police recording decisions, the ideological critique (focusing on working-class street crime). If asked about studying poverty, the mark scheme looks for reference to Townsend’s deprivation index, the debate between validity and reliability, the difficulty of sampling the most deprived households. On a 12-mark Discuss asking how far official statistics are a useful source of data on crime, present the functionalist view (official statistics reflect real patterns of offending and are reliable over time), the interactionist critique (they reflect labelling and police discretion, not true offending patterns) and the Marxist critique (they focus on working-class crime, under-representing corporate and white-collar offending). Close with a supported judgement.
